sentences.text: Pararhabdodon isonensis is the sole species within the extinct genus Pararhabdodon, which belongs to the ornithopod dinosaur group known as hadrosaurids.
This animal was a herbivore that moved on two legs but could also walk on four legs when needed.
The holotype specimen, which serves as the primary example for the species, was estimated to be about 6 meters long.
Studies of the bone tissue suggest this individual had not finished growing, implying the species could reach lengths of roughly 9 meters like its relatives Corythosaurus and Tsintaosaurus.
Although it lived on an island where animals usually become smaller, Pararhabdodon grew quite large, unlike other European hadrosaurs such as Adynomosaurus.
Detailed analysis of the hindlimbs proved that this dinosaur was not the same as Arenysaurus, because their thigh bones were structurally different.
The genus was officially named by Casanovas-Cladellas, Santafé-Llopis, and Isidro-Llorens in the year 1993.
The initial fossils were unearthed at the Sant Romà d'Abella site in Catalonia, Spain, where they were first thought to belong to the genus Rhabdodon.
Excavations at this location began in the spring of 1985, following earlier discoveries by paleontologist Marc Boada in the 1990s near Abella de la Conca.
Pararhabdodon was among the final non-bird dinosaurs to disappear during the mass extinction event at the end of the Cretaceous.
A jawbone found in 2013 showed features typical of the tsintaosaurin tribe, leading to its addition to the species Pararhabdodon isonensis.
Material from the Basturs Poble bonebed was later distinguished from Pararhabdodon because the femurs in those fossils had inconsistent anatomy.
The name Pararhabdodon translates to 'near fluted tooth,' and the animal was originally mistaken for a primitive iguanodontian before being reclassified.
New fossil evidence revealed that Pararhabdodon was actually a hadrosaur rather than a basal iguanodontid, prompting a major reclassification by the original naming team.

In 1999, it was identified as a lambeosaurine hadrosaurid, making it the first of its subfamily in Europe, though later studies questioned this placement and suggested it might be a more primitive hadrosaurid.
This dinosaur lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically in the Maastrichtian stage, between 67 and 66 million years ago in what is now Europe.
The Maastrichtian stage spans from 72.2 to 66 million years ago, covering the final era of the dinosaur age.
A 2019 paper challenged the assignment of specimen MCD 4919 to Pararhabdodon isonensis because its ectopterygoid shelf differed from that of the holotype.
The idea that Pararhabdodon was the first known European lambeosaurine was disputed in 2001 by Jason Head.
It is debated whether the Basturs Poble bonebed represents one species or two, but researchers now lean toward it being a single variable species rather than two distinct ones.
